intro: You are Fauja, a farmer's son in a Punjab village around 1911, with legs too weak to walk until you are five. Your running starts in your late 80s in East London, far from home, with a club and a coach who speaks your language.

sprint.why: Daily training of a long-distance runner: slow, steady kilometres, built up over years.

market.why: Sikh community, club mates and cheering crowds at marathons meant he was never running alone.

office.why: No birth certificate, so records and officials would not confirm his age, however many people saw him run.

stairs.why: Weak legs from early childhood and later age: steep steps cost more energy, so he took them with care.

advantage.title: Steady training
advantage.text: Years of daily running meant Fauja could choose his pace and push when it counted. Roll two dice and take the higher one, twice in your game.

life.title: Punjab, around 1911
life.text: Fauja is born in a Punjab village. He has no birth certificate, so his exact age is never officially confirmed. His legs are so weak that he does not walk until about five.

life.title: Little schooling, no sport
life.text: Other children tease him about his thin legs and he cannot join their games. He gets little schooling and no sport, and becomes a farmer like his family.

life.title: Family and farm
life.text: He marries Gyan Kaur and raises a family while working the land. In the village he is known as modest and kind, with neighbours he can rely on.

life.title: Losses and a new country
life.text: His wife dies in 1992 and a son in 1994. After years of grief, Fauja moves to England to live with another son. In East London he is lonely, and the language is new.

life.title: A club in Ilford
life.text: In Ilford he starts running to cope with grief. At 89 he joins a running club and meets his coach Harmander Singh, a fellow Sikh, who also translates and becomes a friend.

life.title: "Too old"
life.text: Doctors, strangers and even some friends are shocked and say a man his age should rest. People decide what age allows before they ask him. He trains daily, also in cold British weather.

life.title: The first marathon
life.text: In April 2000 Fauja runs his first marathon in London. He finishes, and then goes on to run more marathons, including in New York and Toronto.

q.q: About how old was Fauja Singh at his first marathon?
q.x: He ran the London Marathon in 2000 at 89. He turned 100 (about) in 2011 and finished the Toronto Waterfront Marathon.

life.title: A record at 92
life.text: In 2003, aged 92, he sets a marathon record for his age group in Toronto. His coach, club and a community cheering at the side of the road are with him.

life.title: No paper, no record
life.text: In 2011 he finishes the Toronto marathon at about 100, in just over 8 hours. Guinness World Records does not list it because there is no birth certificate. Many people still honour him, including with a letter from the Queen.

life.title: Torch bearer
life.text: In 2012 Fauja carries the Olympic torch through London at about 100. He also takes part in advertising campaigns and supports charities.

q.q: What did Fauja Singh carry through London in 2012?
q.x: He carried the Olympic torch, and he used his fame to support charities.

life.title: A message for everyone
life.text: His motto: walk, eat simply, be positive. He says age is only a number but also stresses running safely. He ends marathons at 101 with a 10 km race in 2013.

life.title: Home in Punjab
life.text: Fauja Singh dies on 14 July 2025 after a road accident in his home village, at about 114 years old. He leaves a reminder: do not say "you are too old" before you have asked the person.

sources: Guinness World Records statement on age records
flags: Age is unverified (no birth certificate), stated in station 1 and 9.
Station 7 explanation: age at Toronto 2011 is 'about' 100; the 2003 Toronto age-group record is from single-player data.
Stairs zone is an inference from childhood weak legs plus age, not a documented fact; please check.
